frozen_original.title: The Billionaire Cabinet: Howard Lutnick, Scott Bessent, and the Self-Dealing Administration
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump assembled the wealthiest cabinet in American history for his second term, installing billionaires including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (former Cantor Fitzgerald CEO with $800 million in disclosed assets and executive positions in over 800 firms) and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (Key Square Group hedge fund founder with $700 million in assets) in positions overseeing the very markets and regulations that shaped their fortunes. Lutnick's confirmation disclosures revealed $350 million in income over two years from the complex of financial services firms he was supposed to divest. In March 2025, Lutnick told TV viewers Buy Tesla — an explicit endorsement of a company run by a co-president in all but name — which AP and legal experts said violated the 1989 law prohibiting federal employees from using public office for private gain; no action was taken. Bessent admitted in December 2025 that he had failed to divest his soybean farm for 11 months after his ethics agreement pledged he would, only doing so after the Office of Government Ethics formally notified the Senate Finance Committee of his non-compliance. The pattern across the cabinet represented a systematic degradation of conflict-of-interest norms, with the presidency providing cover for officials who openly enriched themselves or their business networks through the exercise of public power.

children.title: Commerce Secretary Lutnick Urges Fox News Viewers to Buy Tesla Stock
children.description_short: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick urged Fox News viewers to buy Tesla stock, prompting federal ethics questions.
children.description_medium: On March 19, 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick urged Fox News viewers to buy Tesla stock. The Washington Post reported the recommendation the next day and described it as an apparent ethics-rule violation. CNBC quoted Lutnick’s on-air recommendation and summarized rules restricting federal employees from using their office to endorse businesses. The sources document the statement and the ethics concern, not an official finding of misconduct or a resulting stock-market effect.
children.description_long: On March 19, 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick appeared on Fox News and urged viewers to buy Tesla stock. The Washington Post reported the recommendation the next day and described it as an apparent violation of federal ethics rules that prohibit officials from endorsing products or businesses. CNBC quoted Lutnick saying, “If you want to learn something on this show tonight, buy Tesla,” and summarized the rule against using a government position or title to endorse a product, service or enterprise. The available reporting establishes the televised recommendation and why it raised ethics questions. It does not establish a formal finding that Lutnick violated the law, an enforcement action, or that the recommendation changed Tesla’s share price. The original combined record also attributed this advice to a wider pattern of cabinet self-dealing and tied it to broad claims about Lutnick’s holdings. Those separate claims are not included in this event card. The documented event is the public recommendation and the ethics concern it prompted; no conclusion about private gain is drawn here. The reviewed sources also do not establish whether Lutnick personally traded Tesla shares after the broadcast.

children.title: Scott Bessent Says He Divested His North Dakota Soybean-Farmland Interest
children.description_short: Scott Bessent said he sold his North Dakota soybean-farmland interest as part of his ethics agreement.
children.description_medium: On December 7, 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he had recently divested his North Dakota soybean-farmland interest under his ethics agreement. The Associated Press reported that the agreement required him to divest his portion of the investment. An August Office of Government Ethics letter described a December 15 target for remaining divestitures and confirmed recusals from matters affecting the assets. The record does not establish a specific farm-sale deadline or an ethics finding about this sale.
children.description_long: On December 7, 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he had recently divested his interest in North Dakota soybean farmland, describing the sale as part of his ethics agreement. The Associated Press reported his remarks on Face the Nation and said the agreement required divestment of his portion of the investment, which was held through a family partnership. Months earlier, the Office of Government Ethics told the Senate Finance Committee that Treasury officials expected remaining asset divestitures by December 15 because the assets were illiquid; the office also said Bessent was recused from particular matters affecting those assets. These sources document Bessent’s reported sale and the broader compliance process. They do not establish that this specific farm remained unsold for exactly eleven months, that a formal OGE notice specifically concerned the farm, or that Bessent acted on a matter affecting it while conflicted. The original card joined the divestiture to Lutnick’s Tesla recommendation, but the events occurred on different dates and concern different officials. This child card keeps the farm divestiture as a separate ethics event and does not characterize it as a finding of corruption or unlawful conduct.

children.description_long: On December 7, 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he had recently divested his interest in North Dakota soybean farmland, describing the sale as part of his ethics agreement. The Associated Press reported his remarks on Face the Nation and said the agreement required divestment of his portion of the investment, which was held through a family partnership. Months earlier, the Office of Government Ethics told the Senate Finance Committee that Treasury officials expected remaining asset divestitures by December 15 because the assets were illiquid; the office also said Bessent was recused from particular matters affecting those assets. These sources document Bessent’s reported sale and the broader compliance process. They do not establish that this specific farm remained unsold for exactly eleven months, that a formal OGE notice specifically concerned the farm, or that Bessent acted on a matter affecting it while conflicted. The original card joined the divestiture to Lutnick’s Tesla recommendation, but the events occurred on different dates and concern different officials. This child card keeps the farm divestiture as a separate ethics event and does not characterize it as a finding of corruption or unlawful conduct.

frozen_original.title: Trump Ends All Federal Support for Minority Business Development
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump administration shut down the Minority Business Development Agency — the only federal agency specifically dedicated to supporting minority-owned businesses — and terminated all federal programs, grants, and technical assistance initiatives that had provided capital access, business counseling, and procurement assistance to minority entrepreneurs. The MBDA had been founded in 1969 and served over 30,000 minority-owned firms annually. Its elimination was part of the broader DEI executive order purge. The administration also ended SBA programs targeted at disadvantaged small businesses including the 8(a) Business Development Program, which had helped minority-owned firms compete for federal contracts. Minority business associations warned the cuts would dramatically widen the racial wealth gap in business ownership.

primary.title: Federal Court Blocks Trump's Order Targeting the Minority Business Agency
primary.description_short: EO 14238 directed MBDA to sharply reduce functions; a federal court later preliminarily enjoined implementation after staff and grant actions.
primary.description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 14238 on March 14, 2025, directing the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate nonstatutory functions and reduce statutory operations and staffing to the legal minimum. The Rhode Island federal court later recorded that most MBDA staff were placed on leave and grants appeared terminated, then granted a preliminary injunction. This account corrects the February date and does not claim all federal minority-business support ended.
primary.description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14238, which directed the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate its nonstatutory components and functions to the maximum extent consistent with law and to reduce statutory functions and staffing to the minimum required by law. The Federal Register text also directed agency heads to report compliance and allowed inconsistent funding requests to be rejected subject to applicable law. The U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island later described MBDA's response: the agency placed all but five employees on paid administrative leave shortly after the order, and the court said it appeared to have terminated existing grant awards in furtherance of the order. The court granted a preliminary injunction against implementing the order as to MBDA; the ruling was preliminary, not a final merits judgment. This narrower entry corrects the frozen record's February date and its claim that all federal minority-business assistance ended. It records the executive directive and documented implementation, not a complete shutdown of every program or the final state of the agency after the injunction. Later agency operations and the injunction's effects are not measured here.

The court granted a preliminary injunction against implementing the order at MBDA. That was a preliminary ruling, not a final merits judgment. The records do not show that all federal minority-business support or SBA programs ended, or establish later agency operations after the injunction.
